content_metadata.description: A detailed tutorial video demonstrating the step-by-step process of preparing a burette for titration in a chemistry lab, including washing, rinsing, filling, and adjusting the burette.

qAndA.question: What color is the titrant used in the video?

qAndA.answer: This position prevents any accidental leaking from the burette.
qAndA.question: Why does the stopcock need to be perpendicular to the glassware when in the closed position?

qAndA.answer: Washing helps to ensure that there are no particles that will interfere with the substances being measured. This helps to guarantee an accurate measurement of the titrant and a more precise calculation of the analyte.
qAndA.question: Why is washing the burette so important?

qAndA.answer: Reading at eye level helps to ensure that the meniscus is viewed directly from the side. This prevents parallax error, which can lead to inaccurate volume measurements.
qAndA.question: Why is it important to read the burette volume at eye level?

qAndA.answer: Coating the inside helps to make sure there is no dilution of the titrant with any remaining drops of distilled water in the burette.
qAndA.question: Why is it important to coat the inside of the burette with titrant?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Welcome to the chemistry lab.
Today we will show you how to prepare your BRF Brite titration.
My name is Brian Ries-Wattis and I'm a biochem major from the class of 2018.
We will outline the procedure from obtaining your BRF to washing and measuring the initial
volume inside it.
We hope that this tutorial will help you out in lab.
Now sit back relax and let's get started.
If your RF is a laboratory apparatus that is used to quantitatively measure the volume
of a liquid or a gas.
The BRF consists of a long graduated glass tube that dispenses liquid.
The amount of liquid that is dispensed from it is controlled by a stopcock which is
located at the bottom of your BRF.
Your rats are typically used in titration experiments.
This is where a solution with a known concentration is used to determine the concentration of another
compound.
In order to properly use a BRF, proper rinsing and washing must be done in order to ensure
there are no molecules or particles that could potentially interfere with what is being
measured.
Washing is essential.
Never assume your glassware is clean.
To do so, rinse your BRF out one to two times with distilled water.
This will cause any particles on the BRF to go into solution and will be washed away.
Once you have filled the BRF, turn the stopcock once and allow some of the water to run through
the dispensing tip.
This allows any air bubbles that are trapped to be dispelled.
Once you have done this, turn the stopcock to the closed position and drain the rest of
the water from the top of the BRF into the sink or a beaker.
Once you have finished rinsing it with DI water, rinse out your BRF once with your titrant
and repeat the same procedure as with water.
Let's now coat the inside of the BRF with the titrant.
Make sure the stopcock is in the closed position with the stopcock perpendicular to the glassware
or about 5ml of titrant using a long stem glass funnel into the BRF and hold the BRF on
its side.
You do not need to fill your BRF to the top just yet.
Using your hands, rotate the glassware providing maximum coverage for the titrant to coat the
inside surface of the glassware.
In this case, the titrant being used is sodium hydroxide.
The last step of washing is essential if you need to be very precise when calculating
the concentration of the titrant.
Now, dispense the last washing into a waste beaker.
Once you are finished with washing, you are now ready to set up your BRF using a long
stem glass funnel and sliding the BRF under eye level carefully pour your titrant into
the BRF to the desired volume.
If you cannot get the BRF to eye level before filling it, you may remove it from the clamp
and hold the BRF to eye level instead.
When doing this, make sure you are very cautious about spilling any titrant on yourself or others.
When reading the initial volume of the BRF, make sure you take the reading at the bottom
of the meniscus.
For opaque liquids, like potassium permanganate, use a flashlight to get a better view of
the meniscus.
If you have overfilled your BRF past the graduations, you may turn your stopcock just a little
bit to dispel some liquid.
Upon reading the initial BRF volume, adjust the BRF height so that there is ample room underneath
the BRF to place an early Meyer flask with the strip pad underneath it.
You may have to adjust the height again to avoid any splashing when dispensing the titrant.
Your BRF is now ready for your experiment.
Thank you for listening and I hope that this video will strengthen your BRF preparation
skills.
